To achieve this, we are working with all clients as One World Bank Group, in close partnership with other multilateral institutions, the private sector, and civil society. The World Bank Group includes:

• International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), which provides financial products and policy advice to help countries reduce poverty and extend the benefits of sustainable growth to all their people. • International Development Association (IDA), which provides grants and concessional loans to low-income countries. • International Finance Corporation (IFC), which mobilizes private capital at scale, supports businesses from microenterprises to large corporations, and creates jobs that drive economic growth and opportunity.

• Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), which houses the World Bank Group Guarantee Platform, providing guarantees to mobilize private capital for developing countries. • International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), which provides international facilities for conciliation, mediation, and arbitration of investment disputes. Our mission is to end extreme poverty and boost shared prosperity on a livable planet. This mission is threatened by multiple, intertwined crises. Time is of the essence. Through the Knowledge Bank and our financial commitments, we are driving impactful development that is:

• Inclusive of everyone, including women and young people.

• Resilient to shocks and fragility.

• Sustainable, through growth and job creation, human development, fiscal and debt management, food security, and access to clean air, water, and affordable energy.

ABOUT US

The World Bank Group Guarantee Platform, hosted at MIGA, continues to play a vital role in bringing private capital to emerging markets. The Board commends MIGA for surpassing $100 billion in cumulative guarantee issuance since its founding in 1988, a remarkable achievement from just $366 million in paid-in capital. In addition, in fiscal 2026, the World Bank Group surpassed its goal of $20 billion in annual guarantee issuance — four years ahead of the 2030 target.

The Board endorsed the extension of the World Bank Group’s Climate Change Action Plan, a significant step that provides vital continuity for countries. The Executive Directors expect the institution to be measured by the tangible impact its work has on communities worldwide, and the Board is grateful for the strong collaboration with Management on this initiative.

Throughout the year, the Board actively engaged with government counterparts, World Bank Group staff, development partners, beneficiaries, civil society organizations, and private sector entities. Delegations of Executive Directors and Alternate Executive Directors undertook five official trips, including visits to West and Central Africa (Sierra Leone and Chad), Latin America and the Caribbean (Dominican Republic, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines), and the Middle East and North Africa (Algeria and Lebanon). Additionally, delegations conducted two thematic trips: to Portugal and Cabo Verde to study the energy transition and sustainable use of marine resources in fostering growth in coastal areas, and to Chile and Argentina, focusing on advancing the energy transition while strengthening water security.

These visits provided invaluable, first-hand insights into country priorities and on-the-ground results, while strengthening connections with clients and the growing number of staff located in the field.

Looking ahead, the Executive Directors and Management share a unified, ambitious vision anchored in a clear set of priorities: delivering on the jobs strategy, disseminating knowledge and expertise through the Knowledge Bank, scaling private capital mobilization, and strengthening operational effectiveness in fragile and conflict-affected settings. While sustained progress ultimately depends on strong country ownership and close collaboration with partners across the international development system, the Board works hand-in-hand with Management to ensure the institution pulls every lever at its disposal. Together, the Board and Management are committed to realizing a more resilient future — one where economic growth creates jobs that deliver dignity, hope, and lasting opportunity.

The Board extends its sincere gratitude to the World Bank Group President, Management, and staff whose tireless efforts are instrumental in advancing these goals, ensuring that progress is transformative and far-reaching.

The Executive Directors support the World Bank Group’s urgent response to these crises while maintaining a resolute focus on the long-term challenge of creating jobs at scale. The Board is encouraged that countries can increasingly access fast-acting finance for emergency response, with 79 countries to date utilizing Crisis Toolkit Arrangements. In fiscal 2026, the Board reaffirmed its support for the World Bank Group’s strategic drive to create more and better-paid jobs as total World Bank Group commitments for the year reached $123.5 billion.1

The Board welcomes the World Bank Group’s new ways of working. By deepening collaboration across our institutions, we are enhancing efficiency and accelerating our impact on the ground. Forging new alliances with private sector partners and clients and strengthening cooperation with development partners ensures that scarce resources are deployed where they can generate the most jobs and growth. Furthermore, the Executive Directors recognize the critical role of the Knowledge Bank — harnessing the institution’s data, analytics, and operational experience — in delivering more impactful, country-led projects. The Board was also pleased this year to approve the creation of a single, independent accountability mechanism, informed by extensive consultations. JOBS ARE ESSENTIAL. THEY PROVIDE DIGNITY, HOPE, AND BELIEF IN A BETTER FUTURE. When jobs are created at scale, they strengthen communities, transform countries, and power the global economy.

Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people will reach working age in developing countries. Those countries are expected to create only about 420 million jobs. Whether this generation becomes an engine of growth or a source of instability will depend in large part on whether they can find productive work.

That is why creating jobs is the overarching focus of the World Bank Group. Three years ago, our shareholders and clients gave us a clear mandate: build a better and bigger World Bank Group — faster, simpler, and better able to bring private capital alongside our own financing and knowledge.

We changed how we work. We shortened average project preparation and approval times from 19 months to nine. We brought the institutions of the World Bank Group together around countries and clients — anchored in one country strategy built around each country’s needs and development priorities. We created a single platform for guarantees, simplified our products and internal structures, developed a purposeful work plan to support the private sector in emerging markets, and replaced a scorecard of 153 indicators with 22 measures focused on results. And we began building vehicles that can connect development projects with investors managing capital at real scale.

Health Works has reached 551.1 million people with quality, affordable health services so that they can lead productive and fulfilling lives. We have also provided nearly 17 million women and women-led businesses with access to capital so they can start, grow, and hire. We aim to support entrepreneurs at all stages — from when they’re first developing a business plan to when they’re hiring their 100th employee. Entrepreneurs power the global economy. And it’s our job to help them do theirs. Technology amplifies our work. We have connected 154 million people to broadband internet and 86 million people to digitally enabled services so they can access markets, improve their skills, use better public services, and participate more fully in the modern economy.

We have fully embraced AI tools at the World Bank Group, and we support clients to adopt, adapt, and then advance them for their own needs. Our client engagements focus on Small AI — affordable, fit-for-purpose solutions designed for local conditions, including places with limited power, connectivity, and computing capacity. This is not a second-best path. It is a practical way to strengthen workers, help firms grow, improve services, support local entrepreneurs, and create more and better jobs. There is much more to do, and no institution can meet the jobs challenge alone. But this year demonstrated what is possible when our shareholders, clients, partners, and staff work together with urgency and purpose.

The World Bank Group is faster, simpler, and better equipped to deliver. Now we must build on that progress — and help create more jobs for more people.

These changes matter because public resources alone cannot meet the need. Our financing and knowledge can help countries build the foundations for growth and create the conditions for investment. But creating jobs at scale requires private businesses. The private sector accounts for 90 percent of jobs globally, the vast majority of them through small- and medium-sized businesses, and entrepreneurs. This year’s results show the progress we have made. We delivered $123.5 billion in financing to clients. We mobilized $112 billion in private capital, more than triple the $35 billion we mobilized in fiscal 2022. Altogether, that brought our total financing and mobilization in developing economies to well over $200 billion in fiscal 2026.

The growth was broad-based. Between fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2026, private capital mobilization nearly tripled in lower-middle-income countries, from $14 billion to $37 billion; more than quadrupled in upper-middle-income countries, from $12 billion to $50 billion; and increased by nearly 150 percent across Africa, from $9 billion to $22 billion. In low-income countries, where private investment is hardest to attract, we deployed our own financing to support development priorities — and mobilized roughly $3 billion in private capital alongside it, extending the reach of our resources and our ability to meet the need in places affected by fragility, conflict, and violence. In short, as we support countries to grow and develop, private capital supplants public capital in driving jobs and growth.

REFORMS AND RESULTS

Three years ago, the World Bank Group launched its reform agenda with a clear ambition: to become a faster, simpler, more effective, and impactful institution — one better equipped to meet the scale and urgency of today’s development challenges. That agenda is now delivering results:

• Private capital mobilization Public capital alone is not enough to tackle the world’s most pressing development challenges. That’s why we mobilized $112 billion in private funds in fiscal 2026 — more than triple the $35 billion mobilized in fiscal 2022 — to further expand opportunity, create jobs, and build infrastructure. We also issued $25 billion in guarantees this year — surpassing our goal of issuing $20 billion annually by 2030 — to give investors the confidence to invest in developing countries. • MDB partnerships The Global Collaborative Co-Financing Platform, of which we are a founding member, has a pipeline of almost 240 projects valued at $140 billion, and we’ve removed co-financing fees to spur even more partnerships. We’ve also agreed to Full Mutual Reliance Frameworks with two multilateral development banks that allow clients to engage with a single lead lender and their operational policies.

• Knowledge transfer We’re applying our data and insights to better help clients create jobs. Assessments such as The Global Jobs Challenge map constraints, reforms, and investment opportunities. The World Bank Group Academy continues to build client capacity with practical, tested development solutions. • Greater efficiency Across the World Bank Group, we’ve consolidated country office leadership and eliminated bureaucratic duplication, making it faster and easier for us to address our clients’ priorities. We cut average project-approval times from 19 months to nine, with some low-risk projects approved in as little as 60 days.

• Corporate initiatives We’re deploying AI to accelerate our work and working with partners to promote AI solutions that are safe and impactful for everyone. We focus on practical applications that solve everyday problems in developing countries. • Clear outcomes Our Scorecard now focuses on 22 key metrics that show how our work creates jobs and improves lives. And our Target Map keeps us ambitious against 10 strategic priorities. We publish our data online, making it more user-friendly and leading to better outcomes. 9

Jobs unlock potential, empower women, engage young people, strengthen communities, create business opportunities and support entrepreneurs, and reduce dependence on development assistance. Giving people the means to move up the ladder of aspirations lifts entire communities out of poverty.

The Knowledge Bank plays a crucial role, bringing decades of frontline experience to provide insight into the reforms that have helped countries and companies thrive.

To multiply our impact, we’re mobilizing affordable, concessional finance through IDA, and private capital through IFC, MIGA, and the World Bank (IBRD/IDA).

But development at scale requires an orchestra — governments, development institutions, philanthropists, and private investors all working in concert. With bold action and a shared commitment, we can turn the promise of future generations into jobs, dignity, and prosperity.

Water security is foundational for productivity and economic growth. As one of the most water-scarce countries in the world, Jordan has struggled to grow its economy and create jobs for its young people. The government of Jordan is taking bold action to boost water security by initiating its largest-ever infrastructure project, the Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project. By 2030, the project is expected to deliver approximately 40 percent of Jordan’s domestic water supply. The project’s construction is directly creating 4,000 jobs and, indirectly, approximately 29,000 jobs, as well as advancing long-term job creation.

The World Bank Group is part of a pool of international lenders providing financing for the project: In fiscal 2026, the Board approved an IFC loan of up to $375 million. IFC is also acting as an accredited entity for a $220 million concessional senior loan and a $75 million investment grant from the Green Climate Fund. For its part, MIGA received Board approval for guarantees of up to $1.25 billion.

Complementing the Aqaba-Amman project is IBRD’s $300 million Jordan Water Sector Efficiency Project, which includes financing from partners. This is strengthening Jordan’s broader water sector through non-revenue water reduction, energy efficiency, and distribution-system readiness. The World Bank Group’s support for Jordan’s water sector aligns with our Water Strategy Implementation Plan, which outlines how investments, long-term policy reforms, and institutional sustainability can deliver water security, economic growth, and job creation.

Attacks to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have created an estimated $91 billion in reconstruction needs. The World Bank Group is supporting the Government of Ukraine to develop a European Union (EU)-aligned energy sector strategy to restore security of supply, reestablish financial viability, mobilize private capital at scale, strengthen corporate governance of state energy companies, and improve financial sustainability — essential ingredients for economic competitiveness, productivity, and employment creation. The World Bank Group is also offering Ukraine comprehensive financial and technical support. Re-PoWER, a World Bank trust fund-financed project, secured $403 million in grants to restore electricity and heating for millions of people. In fiscal 2026, more than $150 million of these grants were allocated for heating units, as well as for equipment needed to secure power imports from the EU.

Another project is rehabilitating hydropower plants and delivering reliable power to affected communities.

In close coordination, IFC’s €50 million financing and support from partners unlocked the private investment to build a new 189 megawatt (MW) wind power plant by the Ukrainian company OKKO, complementing an earlier 147 MW project. The two projects are expected to contribute to Ukraine’s energy grid stability and provide electricity to around 800,000 people. Together with additional renewable energy projects supported by IFC and partners, these private sector investments are expected to add approximately 715 MW of new capacity. The World Bank Group is also promoting private sector resilience in Ukraine.

IBRD is supporting policy reforms across several economic sectors and helping to keep basic services for firms and citizens, while IFC has established risk-sharing facilities with Ukrainian financial institutions to support on-lending to micro, small, and medium enterprises; mobilized private sector participation in infrastructure, including telecom and energy; supported businesses to safeguard jobs and food security; and backed innovation and high-tech ventures through venture capital and private equity funds to retain talent and build future growth. For its part, MIGA has extended and increased guarantees to free up capital linked to two banks’ mandatory reserves, issuing $448 million in new guarantees since February 2022 to keep small businesses afloat and maintain employment opportunities.

Brazil’s family farms employ nearly 10 million people and play a central role in food production. Our partnership with the government, launched in fiscal 2026, aims to support 1 million family farms with improved technology, market logistics, and insurance by 2030. This partnership is part of the World Bank Group’s strategic priority that aims to move 300 million farmers from subsistence to surplus. Our three-pillar strategy leverages the World Bank Group’s unique capabilities. First, the World Bank and IFC strengthen the foundations of family farms by investing in physical and human capital, such as rural roads and research. Then, they align regulations, streamline standards, repurpose subsidies, and remove barriers to doing business. Finally, the World Bank Group expands access to finance through MIGA’s guarantees and insurance, as well as partnerships created by the World Bank and IFC. The private sector is a critical partner across all three pillars.

With this approach, we’ll create an integrated pathway for family farms to access markets, finance, technology, and resilience tools. We’re working quickly because family farms around the world, including 500 million smallholder farmers, produce most of the world’s food, yet many remain in poverty, relying on traditional farming methods and lacking access to markets, finance, and technology. Supporting them to become commercially successful is critical to creating jobs, reducing poverty, and improving global food security. Pacific Island countries face some of the world’s highest rates of premature death and disability from non-communicable disease, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer, alongside persistent communicable diseases. Local healthcare systems struggle to provide care to dispersed populations, and the resulting inefficiencies drive up service costs and hamper job creation and long-term growth.

The World Bank’s Pacific Healthy Islands Transformation (PHIT) project, approved in fiscal 2026, is taking a new approach to improving the health of people across the region. The $239.5 million project covers Fiji, Kiribati, Tonga, and Tuvalu, and — through the Pacific Community — Naoero, Samoa, Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu. Leveraging the expertise of Knowledge Bank teams at the World Bank and IFC, PHIT will create, protect, and safeguard 16,000 vital health and health-support jobs across the Pacific — spanning frontline service delivery, infrastructure development, digital health systems, supply chains, and monitoring and evaluation — representing a major investment in the region’s most critical asset: its people. AI-enabled diagnostics and regional telehealth networks will enable more patients to receive accurate diagnostics; expanded access to specialized services, including regional radiotherapy and advanced medical imaging, will serve patients with specific needs.

Together, these advancements will accelerate regional health and development impact for greater resilience, productivity, and inclusive growth. PHIT is the largest World Bank Group multi-country operation in the Pacific and supports our strategic priority of delivering quality, affordable health services to 1.5 billion people by 2030. It is also the first project developed with the Asian Development Bank under the Full Mutual Reliance Framework, helping reduce transaction costs. The OPEC Fund and the Pandemic Fund are also co-financing PHIT, which is set to help Pacific Island countries establish the fundamental conditions for good health, jobs, and growth.

Tourism is an engine of Cabo Verde’s economy, accounting for over a quarter of GDP. But for years, the sector has been constrained by a narrow model dominated by all-inclusive resorts in only two of the archipelago’s 10 islands, with few links to local businesses. Infrastructure deficits, a shortage of skilled hospitality workers, and the absence of a coherent framework for attracting quality investment left the country exposed and its potential unrealized.

The World Bank Group has worked across its private and public sector arms to help Cabo Verde chart a more diversified and inclusive tourism sector. Two World Bank operations — the Resilient Tourism and Blue Economy Development Project and the Improving Connectivity and Urban Infrastructure Project — are strengthening the sector’s governance and institutional framework, while upgrading critical infrastructure, including coastal and jetty facilities, maritime passenger terminals, heritage sites, and public spaces. Two other programs — the Human Capital Development Project and the Health Security Program in Western and Central Africa — are complementing these efforts by strengthening essential services. Together they support more than 100 vocational and specialty training courses, translating growth into more and better-paid jobs.

IFC has anchored the private sector transformation. In December 2023, IFC arranged a financing package of up to €35.5 million for Oásis Atlântico, one of the country’s leading hospitality operators. The investment supports more than 700 direct jobs and 20,000 indirect jobs, and linkages with over 700 small suppliers and farmers. IFC has also extended two successive sustainability-linked loans to Cabo Verde Airports S.A., a subsidiary of VINCI Airports, with the most recent reaching up to €60 million in February 2026. The financing has modernized and greened the country’s seven airports, created over 2,000 direct jobs and 1,200 indirect jobs, and helped establish 35 new air routes — driving a 60 percent surge in passenger volumes since 2022.

The results are reshaping Cabo Verde’s tourism landscape. Average daily tourist spending and overnight stays in previously under-visited islands are both rising, and growing private investment signals confidence in the country’s trajectory. With the World Bank Group supporting the full arc from governance and infrastructure to skills and private finance, Cabo Verde is building a more diversified, sustainable, and job-rich tourism economy.

India aspires to become an upper-middle-income economy in the next decade. Its National Green Hydrogen Mission, which aims to catalyze 600,000 jobs by 2030, is critical to meeting this goal.

Since 2021, the World Bank Group has helped India advance hydrogen hub planning, enabling infrastructure, and public-private engagement to mobilize private sector investment. In fiscal 2026, IFC invested $25 million in Hygenco Green Energies — its first direct green hydrogen investment in India. This investment is complemented by two IFC-managed blended finance facilities, the Clean Technology Fund ($20 million) and the Frontier Opportunities Fund ($5 million), which altogether enabled $55 million in co-investment from other private sector partners.

The total financing package, including equity from other partners, will support the creation of more than 1,000 direct and indirect jobs across the green hydrogen value chain and broader industrial ecosystem over the next five years.

This follows two previous financing commitments from the World Bank, totaling $3 billion, to help India accelerate the development of low-carbon energy. By promoting the development of a vibrant market for green hydrogen, the World Bank Group is helping to create jobs, strengthen India’s manufacturing base, and support long-term economic growth.

BUSINESS OVERVIEW PRIVATE CAPITAL MOBILIZATION AND JOBS The World Bank Group is adapting to meet the scale of the jobs challenge, shifting from a provider of finance to a platform that channels global capital flows into developing countries. Rather than relying principally on our balance sheets, we are increasingly using financing, guarantees, data, and our convening role to crowd private capital into the most productive sectors for job creation. This means building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms that allow risk to be distributed across a broader set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool of global capital to development opportunities. In fiscal 2026, we made real progress and changes that are already translating into results. While financing from the World Bank Group’s own resources rose from $98 billion to $123.5 billion over the last five years, private capital mobilization surged from $35 billion in fiscal 2022 to $112 billion in fiscal 2026.

This more than threefold increase represents a fundamental shift in our ability to bring external capital into development opportunities at scale, making us the largest mobilizer of private capital among multilateral development banks. Guarantees issued by the World Bank Group Guarantee Platform grew by 46 percent in fiscal 2026. We are providing patient equity in markets where early-stage capital is scarce and expanding local-currency financing where foreign-exchange risk would otherwise deter investment. We also began piloting “originate-to-distribute” approaches to connect institutional investors with emerging market assets at greater scale. And we’re providing investors and ratings agencies with historical data on the performance of emerging market lending through the Global Emerging Markets Risk Database. These practical shifts are already supporting investment and jobs.

A NEW APPROACH TO COUNTRY ENGAGEMENT We are building a One World Bank Group client coverage model that aligns public and private sector solutions around jobs, growth, and private investment. Our new approach is more efficient, outcome-focused, and systematic in tapping private sector solutions and will help countries tackle their development challenges with greater speed, quality, and impact.

The centerpiece of this new approach is our Country Partnership Framework (CPF) — the key tool that guides our strategic engagement with countries. CPFs typically span four to six years, with a maximum duration of 10 years, to align our support with a country’s development goals and the World Bank Group Scorecard.

In fiscal 2026, we delivered 28 new CPFs that are underpinned by five core diagnostics: Country Climate and Development Reports, Country Growth and Jobs Reports, Country Private Sector Diagnostics, Poverty and Equity Assessments, and Public Finance Reviews. From this data, we identify three to five outcomes that support job creation, and complementary public and private actions to support the outcomes. With outcomes defined at the intersection of three selectivity criteria — development challenges, country development goals, and World Bank Group comparative advantages — CPFs serve as the primary vehicle for translating World Bank Group targets and strategies into country-level action, delivering on client priorities through complementary public and private solutions.

We also conducted our first cross-World Bank Group business planning exercise in fiscal 2026. We intend to make this an annual event so we can better respond to government needs and adapt our programs to evolving country contexts.

TRUST FUNDS The World Bank Group manages a diverse portfolio of trust funds, which receive resources from more than 100 donors. Trust funds are part of the World Bank Group’s toolkit and complement its core financing.

They can mobilize funding quickly to fill financing gaps, offset risks, and provide flexibility. This often means the World Bank Group can work in the most challenging environments and deliver impact even where core financing is limited or unavailable. Trust funds broaden World Bank Group partnerships to more effectively address country, regional, and global challenges. Trust funds also serve as force multipliers for the World Bank Group’s development impact, enabling IBRD to build public sector foundations, IFC to catalyze private investment, and MIGA to de-risk both. This integrated approach unlocks private investment and delivers results at scale by leveraging each institution’s unique strengths while working cohesively toward shared development objectives. While trust funds can vary in size and scope, they all serve the World Bank Group’s mission to end extreme poverty and boost shared prosperity on a livable planet.

The World Bank uses trust funds to strengthen the public sector foundations essential for development. At the end of fiscal 2026, World Bank trust funds held $27.9 billion in trust as cash, investments, and promissory notes. In the last five years (fiscal 2022–26), 91 percent ($67.2 billion) of World Bank trust fund disbursements went to recipient-executed activities in member countries, helping to build the foundations for job growth including infrastructure, institutions, and human capital. Of this amount, over $8.1 billion was disbursed to IDA and IDA-blend countries (i.e., countries eligible for both IDA and IBRD lending). Trust funds serve as engines of innovation, funding about two-thirds of the World Bank’s advisory services and analytics that lay the groundwork for both public and private investment.

CATALYZING PRIVATE SECTOR INVESTMENT While the World Bank builds public sector foundations, IFC catalyzes private sector investment, mobilizing private capital with support from development partners. In fiscal 2026, IFC deployed nearly $1.4 billion in partner funding across its blended finance, upstream, and advisory activities, helping transform markets, mobilize investment, and support job creation in challenging environments. This sustained donor support reflects the strength of IFC’s longstanding relationships with development partners.

IFC’s blended finance trust funds provide concessional donor funding, combining it with IFC’s own-account financing to make high-impact projects viable in challenging markets. On average, from fiscal 2018–2026, every dollar of blended finance helped unlock more than $6 in total investment. Approximately 41 percent of partner contributions to IFC blended finance trust funds signed in fiscal 2026 will support private sector development in fragile and conflict-affected situations, demonstrating how trust funds enable IFC to operate where risks are highest and needs are greatest. Tailored blended finance solutions, including several innovative approaches introduced or expanded during the year, helped advance projects that could not proceed on commercial terms alone.

To support Ukraine’s private sector, IFC and the European Commission established the first High Impact Equity Guarantee Program for Ukraine to mobilize equity investment, including in infrastructure and small and medium enterprises, with strong potential for replication in other emerging markets. Also in fiscal 2026, Italy joined eight other IFC development partners — Belgium, the European Commission, France, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom — to support IFC’s investment program in Ukraine, which helps sustain critical sectors and supports Ukraine’s reconstruction, including agribusiness, energy, and technology, and enables businesses to continue operating despite security risks, labor shortages, and rising input costs. IFC trust funds have now received more than $1 billion in concessional finance commitments for Ukraine.

The Catalytic First Loss Guarantee Program (CFLG) under IFC’s Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Finance Platform illustrates how close World Bank Group collaboration can expand financing for MSMEs, one of IFC’s key priorities. Supported by the IDA Private Sector Window trust fund, this program provides guarantees to private financial intermediaries. In fiscal 2026, the program fully deployed its Board-approved $20 million CFLG envelope trust fund allocation alongside $22 million of IFC own-account financing, together mobilizing $224 million in total financing — including $202 million in private capital — an 11-fold multiple of the trust fund allocation, and demonstrating the potential to further scale private investment in MSME finance.

Germany became the first donor to the Frontier Opportunities Fund, a novel financing vehicle that uses concessional first-loss capital to improve risk-return profiles and catalyze equity investment and philanthropic co-investments in high-impact climate projects across developing and emerging markets.

IFC advisory and upstream trust funds complement the World Bank’s public sector work by helping to de-risk projects, develop investable opportunities, and support reforms that attract private capital into markets where it might otherwise remain on the sidelines. These trust-funded activities bridge public sector reforms and private sector investment. In fiscal 2026, $178 million of development partner funding was spent on advisory services and upstream activities. Donor trust funds accounted for 43 percent of IFC’s total upstream and advisory resources, supporting shared World Bank Group priorities, including the jobs agenda and private capital mobilization. IFC’s upstream work helped enable $23.6 billion in long-term financing for private sector projects — more than one-quarter of all long-term financing committed by IFC and its partners during the year.

In fiscal 2026, IFC’s trust-funded upstream and advisory work advanced job-creating projects in high-impact sectors such as infrastructure, agribusiness, and value-added manufacturing, including in fragile and conflict-affected situations. In Bangladesh, Australia supported the Laldia Container Terminal public-private partnership (PPP) through IFC’s South Asia Regional Infrastructure and Connectivity trust fund. IFC’s PPP transaction advisory work helped structure the project and mobilized more than $760 million in private investment. The project is expected to generate more than 3,000 jobs, including 500-700 direct positions at the terminal, plus significant indirect employment in logistics and manufacturing.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the United Kingdom, through a new trust fund contribution, supported IFC’s Scaling Finance for Agribusinesses program, which aims to create jobs and improve livelihoods by expanding access to finance, agricultural equipment, and business opportunities for women entrepreneurs, smallholder farmers, and agricultural small businesses. In Ukraine, the Japan-IFC Comprehensive Trust Fund is supporting the development of the NovaSklo Greenfield project, which aims to establish the country’s first domestic float-glass manufacturing facility through feasibility, risk, environmental and social, and corporate governance reviews; financial modeling; and prospective investor engagement. Once operational, it is expected to support Ukraine’s reconstruction by reducing reliance on imports, creating more than 300 direct jobs, and generating additional employment across related value chains.

DE-RISKING THROUGH GUARANTEES MIGA completes the World Bank Group’s integrated approach by using trust funds to provide guarantee instruments that de-risk investments for both public and private sector projects. Trust funds, including the Renewable Energy Catalyst Trust Fund, the West Bank and Gaza Trust Fund, and the Support for Ukraine’s Reconstruction and Economy Trust Fund, share guarantee exposure on individual projects via first-loss layers and reinsurance. These instruments enable MIGA to bridge the World Bank’s public sector work and IFC’s private sector investments by guaranteeing higher-risk projects and increasing investor confidence, particularly in fragile and conflict-affected settings, while advancing job creation and women’s economic empowerment. The Fund for Advancing Sustainability complements these efforts by strengthening environmental, social, and gender practices and broadening access to guarantees for small businesses in low-income and fragile countries.

IBRD FINANCIAL RESOURCES AND FINANCIAL MODEL IBRD finances its loans through its own equity and by borrowing in the capital markets via the issuance of IBRD bonds to fund development projects in member countries. IBRD is rated triple-A by both Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s, and investors view its bonds as high-quality and liquid securities. IBRD’s funding approach continues to aim to achieve the best long-term value for borrowing members on a sustainable basis. IBRD’s ability to channel the funds it raises in international capital markets to developing member countries is important in achieving its goals.

IBRD’s approach has enabled it to borrow at favorable market terms and pass the savings on to its borrowing members. Funds not immediately deployed for lending are held in IBRD’s investment portfolio to provide liquidity for its operations. In fiscal 2026, IBRD raised nearly $50 billion by issuing medium- and long-term bonds in a variety of currencies.

As a cooperative institution, IBRD does not seek to maximize profit but rather to earn enough income to ensure the long-term financial capacity necessary to sustain its development activities. Allocable net income in fiscal 2026 was $2.3 billion, and out of this, the Executive Directors approved the allocation of $1.1 billion to the General Reserve, and recommended to the Board of Governors an allocation of $750 million to IDA and $500 million to Surplus. Further, the Board recommended to IBRD’s Board of Governors the following transfers out of Surplus: $300 million to the IBRD Trust Fund for Gaza and West Bank, $100 million to the Grant Facility for Project Preparation, and $100 million to the IBRD Surplus-Funded Livable Planet Fund. As part of its lending, borrowing, and investment activities, IBRD is exposed to market, counterparty, country credit, and operational risks.

The World Bank Group’s Chief Risk Officer (CRO) leads the risk oversight function covering financial, operational, model, and environmental and social risks. The CRO also supports the institutional decision-making process through dedicated risk committees that cover financial, operational, and franchise risks. In addition, IBRD has implemented a strong risk management framework to support management in its oversight functions. The framework is designed to enable and support IBRD in achieving its goals in a financially sustainable manner. One summary measure of IBRD’s risk profile is equity-to-loans ratio, which is closely managed in line with its financial and risk outlook. As of June 30, 2026, this ratio was 21.6 percent, and IBRD’s cumulative subscribed capital totaled $332.5 billion, including $23.6 billion in paid-in capital.

NOTEWORTHY IN FISCAL 2026 The World Bank (IBRD/IDA) offers a variety of financing instruments and approaches to help countries achieve their development goals. These include:

• Investment Project Financing, which helps build physical and social infrastructure and develop institutional capacity;

• Development Policy Financing, which supports policy and institutional reforms, including through policy-based guarantees; and

• Program-for-Results Financing, which links the disbursement of funds to the achievement of predefined results. In fiscal 2026, we approved 58 Development Policy Financing operations, totaling $24.2 billion; 62 Program-for-Results operations, of which 13 were additional financing, totaling $15.8 billion; and 251 Investment Project Financing operations, of which 81 were additional financing, totaling $40.9 billion. Our own-account climate co-benefits reached $48 billion in fiscal 2026, representing 44 percent of total World Bank commitments, including 30 percent for Development Policy Financing, 38 percent for Program-for-Results, and 54 percent for Investment Project Financing. We also mobilized a record $48 billion in climate co-benefits through private sector financing, bringing the combined total to nearly $96 billion, up 21 percent from fiscal 2025.

Our Multiphase Programmatic Approach (MPA) enables countries to structure long, large, or complex engagements as a set of smaller, complementary Investment Project Financing and Program-for-Results operations within a single program. This approach facilitates both vertical programs, which involve in-depth, sustained engagement within a single country, and horizontal programs, which encompass multiple countries, states within a country, or subnational entities. In fiscal 2026, the World Bank approved 33 new programs totaling $25.1 billion in financing, comprising 15 vertical programs ($8.2 billion) and 18 horizontal programs ($16.9 billion). Total MPA project approvals comprised 95 projects totaling $17.7 billion, including nine additional financing projects totaling $1.0 billion. As of June 2026, a total of 80 countries have implemented at least one instrument from the Crisis Preparedness and Response Toolkit.
With those instruments, countries have pre-arranged contingent resources and catastrophe bonds/insurance, allowing them to focus on disaster recovery.

PROCUREMENT FRAMEWORK In fiscal 2026, we worked closely with borrowers and the private sector to enhance World Bank-financed operational procurement. We built on the existing requirement to include “rated criteria” — non-price factors to evaluate quality — by mandating a minimum quality weighting of 50 percent for most international procurement.

We also now require early market engagement for contracts with an estimated value at or over $10 million to help attract high-caliber bidders and optimize procurement strategies. To support local jobs, bidders for international civil works contracts must now allocate at least 30 percent of total labor costs to local labor, helping generate local employment while promoting skills development. New digital tools are also simplifying access to opportunities and improving procurement data collection, including an AI tool that helps the private sector identify World Bank-financed operational procurement. 59

We have increased our outreach to the private sector, with nearly 200 procurement engagements across all regions. Procurement activities often involve long lead times so the full impact of these changes will take time, though results from the first year of implementation are promising.

NOTEWORTHY IN FISCAL 2026 BUILDING NEW AND IMPROVED PLATFORMS FOR MOBILIZING PRIVATE CAPITAL Large institutional investors, such as pension funds, insurance companies, and asset managers, typically allocate capital through standardized asset classes and systematic distribution rather than for individual transactions. IFC’s originate-to-distribute business model is designed to meet those needs by creating diversified packages of assets — across multiple projects and markets — that are structured in a form that is recognizable and can be in some cases independently rated. The originate-to-distribute pathway includes existing mobilization products with significant investor engagement, such as B loans, while broadening IFC’s approach to investor participation through more systematic and standardized channels of distribution, including securitization.

In September 2025, IFC launched the Emerging Markets Securitization Program (EMSP), a significant step forward in our originate-to-distribute program. EMSP recycles IFC’s loans into packaged securities in which investors such as asset managers, pension funds, and insurance companies can invest. The $510 million transaction was listed on the London Stock Exchange, giving visibility, pricing transparency, liquidity, and the prospect of secondary trading. The second transaction under the EMSP was completed in June 2026, demonstrating its ability to replicate and scale. These transactions benefited from a catalytic equity co-investment from the UK Government’s Mobilist Program alongside IFC. IFC further expanded its originate-to-distribute program in fiscal 2026 with the inaugural Trade Finance Synthetic Securitization (TFSS).

The TFSS is composed of $500 million trade assets originated under IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program, which has more than half its portfolio in low-income and fragile and conflict-affected states. The transaction’s private capital mobilization ratio is up to 1:19, meaning for every dollar of risk retained by IFC, up to $19 are taken up by private investors.

The originate-to-distribute model that underpins the EMSP and TFSS can be standardized and scaled, providing an efficient means to draw substantially more private capital into emerging markets. IFC also continued to build upon proven platforms for mobilizing private capital at scale. One of the most effective is the Managed Co-Lending Portfolio Program (MCPP), a portfolio syndications platform through which investors can gain exposure to a diverse mix of loans to private sector borrowers in emerging markets. In fiscal 2026, the MCPP mobilized $6 billion from 19 global insurers to support lending to financial institutions in emerging markets. By sharing the credit risk on a portion of IFC’s loan portfolio, the program frees up balance sheet capacity and is expected to support up to $10 billion in new IFC financing to small- and medium-sized enterprises. It is IFC’s largest mobilization under a single agreement.

ADDRESSING THE SHORTAGE OF EQUITY IN EMERGING MARKET FIRMS Equity is the scarcest form of financing in emerging markets and the foundation for sustainable business growth. IFC is working to increase its own equity investments while developing new ways to bring equity from other investors into developing economies.

IFC has expanded its capacity to deploy junior equity by investing $100 million of its net income to seed the Frontier Opportunities Fund. The fund allows IFC to take on more complex risk positions and crowd in private capital, including senior equity, to unlock investments in the most challenging markets. Eight projects have been Board-approved. As of June 30, 2026, an additional $100 million has been allocated to the Frontier Opportunities Fund, allowing IFC to meet the burgeoning pipeline of projects. The portfolio covers a wide range of sectors, including carbon finance, energy access and transition, green hydrogen, and industrial transformation.

EXTENDING MORE CAPITAL AND SUPPORT TO MSMEs Reaching micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises is central to the jobs challenge. These businesses are the largest employers in developing economies, yet they are often the hardest to serve. IFC is expanding its reach through digital platforms, supply chain integration, and tailored financing — going beyond financial institutions to connect entrepreneurs more directly to capital and markets. Integrating into supply chains can propel growth for smaller enterprises. To that end, a new risk-sharing facility launched in fiscal 2026 with Standard Chartered is designed to strengthen supply chains for businesses across Africa. The partnership introduces supply chain finance solutions in eight markets: Côte d’Ivoire, Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania, and Zambia.

Over the next three years, it is projected to enable about $1.9 billion in supply chain finance transactions, supporting more than 500 suppliers in both domestic and global value chains.

CREATING MARKETS IN FRAGILE AND CONFLICT-AFFECTED COUNTRIES Fragile, conflict-affected, and violence-affected (FCV) countries are where the private sector gap is widest and the need for jobs most urgent. By 2030, nearly 60 percent of the world’s extreme poor will live in FCV countries. The World Bank Group’s FCV Strategy, launched in fiscal 2026, is the institution’s five-year response, with IFC leading on efforts to mobilize private investment in the markets where it is most scarce.

IFC is the largest development finance institution in fragile and conflict-affected situations and, in line with the broader World Bank Group strategy, IFC’s approach is calibrated to context. In improving markets, IFC takes 69

on risk to build investor confidence and establish track records that draw in private capital. In deteriorating markets, we focus on keeping essential functions running, including trade finance, payment systems, and the supply of critical goods. IFC’s Upstream and Advisory work is especially key to market creation in these settings, laying the groundwork and developing projects in markets that commercial finance has yet to reach.

The tools backing this approach are concrete. The Small Loan Guarantee Program has backed lending across 34 IDA and European Commission eligible countries with a focus on fragile and conflict-affected states. The Frontier Opportunities Fund provides early-stage equity in markets too early for conventional investment. A new $100 million Concessional Capital Window serves fragile middle-income countries and refugee-hosting economies. And the IDA Private Sector Window has been streamlined to deploy blended finance faster. In Ukraine, blended concessional finance contributions from development partners have reached more than $1 billion this year and have been instrumental in enabling IFC to take on greater risk, which in turn mobilizes additional private capital. Moreover, the Local Champions Initiative, an IFC program designed to identify and support promising local entrepreneurs, shows how these tools scale, building a replicable pipeline of investable local firms.

Across the Sahel, the initiative has already enabled $55.4 million in IFC financing.

ENHANCING CREDIT RISK TRANSPARENCY A persistent barrier to private investment in emerging markets is the mismatch between perceived and actual risk. The Global Emerging Markets Risk Database (GEMs) Consortium — the largest source of credit risk data for investments in emerging markets and developing economies — addresses this directly by providing hard data that allows investors and rating agencies to assess risk more accurately and price it more fairly. As confidence in emerging market asset quality grows, so does the potential to attract institutional capital at scale.

The Consortium was created in 2009 on the initiative of the European Investment Bank and IFC and has evolved into a community of practice that develops common approaches and data methodologies to record default and recovery frequencies for the member multilateral development banks and development finance institutions. In fiscal 2026, GEMs released three updated reports: Default and Recovery Statistics: Private Lending 1994–

2024; Default and Recovery Statistics: Public Lending 1994–2024; and Default and Recovery Statistics: Sovereign and Sovereign-guaranteed Lending 1984–2024. These offer new, more granular statistics, providing investors and other GEMs users with greater insights and more information. MEASURING WHAT MATTERS IN DEVELOPMENT IMPACT Development impact is a core component of IFC’s mandate. IFC prioritizes rigorous measurement, monitoring, and evaluation of the development impact of its investment and advisory operations.

When making investment decisions, IFC systematically weighs development impact alongside financial returns, risks, and alignment with strategic objectives and priorities, with a particular focus on fostering opportunities for underserved populations in emerging and underdeveloped markets. To that end, IFC developed its impact management tool — the Anticipated Impact Measurement and Monitoring (AIMM) system.8 For the past eight years, IFC has been assessing the development impact of all our investments and assigning each an impact rating (Excellent, Good, Satisfactory, Low) to inform investment decisions.

The AIMM ratings for investment projects at entry have improved as IFC has increasingly focused more on high-impact areas such as low-income countries, climate, small businesses, and other thematic priorities such as working with underserved and vulnerable populations. In fiscal 2026, IFC committed 341 AIMM-assessed investment projects with 96 percent of them rated Good or Excellent — one percentage point higher than the previous fiscal year. IFC also monitors active projects in the portfolio and tracks key development impact indicators to allow us to take corrective action when projects are off track. In fiscal 2026, 65 percent of the 1,570 projects in the AIMM portfolio were rated Good or Excellent, compared to 62 percent in fiscal 2025. We also conduct comprehensive assessment of project development impact at the end of the project’s implementation period.

In fiscal 2026, 45 percent of the 168 projects that completed their implementation in that year were rated Good or Excellent, representing 49 percent of the corresponding commitment volume. Changes in impact ratings during implementation have been associated primarily with country and macroeconomic factors, with client, and market or industry factors also playing a role.

The development impact of all our investments is monitored using outcome indicators identified for each project at the time of approval, including indicators that track their impact on their ultimate expected beneficiaries. For example, we track the number and volume of loans provided by financial intermediaries to small businesses; the number of farmers that benefit from improved access to inputs, product markets, finance, or better farming practices; the number of patients that receive health services; the number of students that receive access to education; the growth in access to infrastructure services; and the greenhouse gas emissions that are avoided thanks to new technologies. Examples of the preliminary results achieved by our fiscal 2026 active portfolio include:

The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) supports cross-border investment by offering an independent, specialized forum for the resolution of disputes. Effective, impartial dispute resolution strengthens confidence among investors and States and enhances predictability — core pillars of a favorable investment landscape. ICSID is a unique institution, created by the Convention on the Settlement of Investment Disputes between States and Nationals of Other States. This multilateral agreement, also known as the ICSID Convention, was formulated in 1965 by the Executive Directors of the World Bank. ICSID is essential to the World Bank Group’s work to accelerate job creation at scale, a strategy focused on investing in the physical and human infrastructure that people and businesses need to thrive, supporting business-enabling environments, and mobilizing private capital.

By providing an effective, impartial forum for resolving international investment disputes, ICSID mitigates perceived risk and encourages the mobilization of private capital across borders. The availability of ICSID to investors and States fosters trust and predictability, helping create investment environments that drive economic growth and job creation.

At the core of this work are ICSID’s dispute administration services, which cover a range of procedures including arbitration, conciliation, mediation, and fact-finding for disputes arising from investment contracts, international treaties, and domestic investment laws. ICSID’s rules and procedures are widely regarded as the gold standard for investment dispute settlement, offering a stable and predictable legal framework that balances the interests of both States and investors and has been modernized over time to reflect best practices in the field. ICSID also supports the development of international investment law and dispute settlement by producing and sharing knowledge, building capacity, and engaging with Member States and other stakeholders on investment dispute prevention, management, and settlement.

Fiscal 2026 saw meaningful progress across all these areas, as ICSID advanced its priorities to deepen engagement and knowledge, expand mediation and amicable settlement, and uphold the highest standards in case management.

On March 6, 2026, President Nasry Juan Asfura of Honduras signed the ICSID Convention in Washington, D.C., making Honduras the 166th Signatory State to the Convention. ICSID Membership has steadily expanded since the ICSID Convention opened for signature in 1965. By the early 2000s, 149 States had signed the ICSID Convention, and 132 of those had ratified it. ICSID membership is considered a positive factor in MIGA’s risk assessment for insurance guarantees and the World Bank Group’s overall assessment of countries’ investment landscape. ICSID membership supports States’ policies to attract and retain foreign direct investment to create more job opportunities and economic growth. It signals States’ openness to resolving disputes through arbitration, conciliation, and mediation in a trusted forum established under an international convention. There is no cost to join or maintain membership in ICSID.

In fiscal 2026, ICSID published its first in-depth study on contract-based investment dispute resolution, drawing on an analysis of 175 cases registered under the ICSID Convention and Additional Facility. Of the arbitrations concluded in fiscal 2026, 63 percent were decided by a tribunal and 37 percent were settled or otherwise discontinued, broadly reflecting ICSID’s long-term trend of arbitration outcomes. Among disputes decided by tribunals in the past year, 37 percent of awards upheld claims in part or in full, 40 percent rejected all claims on the merits, 18 percent declined jurisdiction, and 5 percent of cases were dismissed for manifest lack of legal merit.

In ICSID arbitrations, financial compensation is typically the primary remedy claimants seek for alleged breaches of investment obligations. Investors typically seek damages for harm they claim to have suffered as a result of measures adopted by the host State. The amounts claimed and awarded can vary significantly depending on the nature of the investment and dispute at issue.

In fiscal 2026, 70 percent of arbitration cases decided by tribunals resulted in no damages awarded to claimants, whether due to jurisdictional dismissals, findings of no liability, or liability without damages. During fiscal 2026, ICSID administered 256 sessions, hearings, and meetings. Parties and tribunals chose from in-person, virtual, or hybrid formats based on the needs of each case, with 75 percent of hearings and sessions incorporating remote features supported by ICSID’s audio and video conferencing facilities. Of all the in-person hearings in fiscal 2026, 44 percent were held at ICSID’s hearing center in Washington, D.C., with the remainder taking place at venues agreed upon by the parties: Paris (30 percent), London (12 percent), Singapore (5 percent), and other locations (9 percent).

ICSID continued to see a diverse pool of arbitrators, conciliators, and committee members in fiscal 2026. The Centre recorded 250 appointments to ICSID cases, the second highest number in a single fiscal year. Appointees represented 52 different nationalities, and 29 percent of all appointments were nationals from low- or middle-income economies. First-time appointees accounted for 8 percent of all appointments; among them, 25 percent were nationals of low- or middle-income economies and 35 percent were women.

The ICSID Secretariat comprises 76 staff members representing 39 nationalities and speaking 22 languages, providing professional legal, administrative, and financial services across all cases. Each case is assigned a dedicated management team led by an experienced legal counsel and supported by paralegals and legal assistants. A finance and administration team oversees the financial aspects of cases and manages the planning and logistics of ICSID sessions and hearings, while an institutional matters team handles ICSID membership and the Centre’s publication program.
